verdict: Avoid new wholesale-trade exposure in Guwahati for now; lend only to fast-moving FMCG/staples distributors with clean receivables and full fire cover, and decline discretionary-goods and slow-inventory traders.
title: Guwahati Wholesale Trade: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business actually is
**A Guwahati wholesaler buys stock in bulk, warehouses it, and sells on short credit to retailers and semi-wholesalers across the Brahmaputra valley.** Cash is made on turnover and margin per cycle, not on price; the balance sheet is mostly inventory and receivables, with little fixed capex beyond godown and vehicles. So when a proposal lands, check the stock-turn and receivable days first, because that is where the money is tied.

## What has changed now
**Local demand has visibly softened: Durga Puja vendors in Guwahati report fewer footfalls and falling sales [1].** That is a festival-season read, not a full-year number, so treat it as a warning on discretionary stock. Input costs are also moving: milk in Guwahati rises by Rs 2 per litre from 1 November [2]. **Assam's electricity demand grew only 1.9% Apr-to-date against India's 9.5% [D], a local activity signal that sits against a strong state GST number of +36.9% [D].** The two point in opposite directions, so ask the borrower which end-market they actually serve.

## The growth pocket to pursue
**Pursue distributors of daily-consumption staples and FMCG lines, where the milk price pass-through [2] shows pricing power exists in essentials.** Peer evidence supports wholesale as a live channel: Aditya Birla Lifestyle's wholesale channel grew 18% in Q2 [7], and Mishka Exim's June 2026 net sales rose 234.87% YoY on trading volumes [5] — though its gross margin was only 11.5% [5], which tells you thin-margin trading needs volume and clean collections to work. **Avoid traders in slow-moving discretionary goods and any single-godown operator without fire cover, given a Hatigaon wholesale shop fire with losses estimated up to Rs 1 crore [3].**

## How to grow safely
**Structure limits against stock and receivables, not against turnover, and take monthly stock statements plus insurance endorsements in the bank's name.** CRISIL flags inventory obsolescence and receivable collection as the core trading risks [9][10], so when a proposal lands, check receivable days against scale; if collections stretch, ask for the ageing ledger and the top-five buyer list. **Take GST returns monthly and match them to stock and sales, because the state GST surge [D] makes under-reporting easy to hide.** Keep tenors short and renew annually.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for falling festival-season sales repeating beyond Puja [1], rising stock days, and any drop in the borrower's own electricity or godown activity.** If a borrower's sales fall while state GST rises [D], ask why before renewing. If fire cover lapses or stock is uninsured, stop enhancement until reinstated [3]. Note that the peer and rating sources here are undated or foreign-market; lean on the local news and the data pack.
watch: Stock days rise beyond the borrower's own six-month average -> freeze limit enhancement and inspect godown
GST-paid sales fall while Assam GST grows +36.9% [D] -> ask for buyer-wise ledger before renewal
Cover lapsed or godown uninsured -> stop enhancement until reinstated [3]
Repeat of falling Puja footfalls [1] into next season -> shift limit to staples-only borrowers
